specious

SPEE-shus -- from Latin speciosus ('good-looking, plausible'), from species ('appearance'). · adjective

Hear It

What It Means

Specious is falsely appearing to be right, true, or fair.

During the debate tournament, the freshman team won several early rounds with specious arguments that impressed the judges but collapsed under real scrutiny.

Example

The ad's specious claim that the vitamin could 'boost your brainpower by 40 percent' relied on a single study of eight mice.

Notice specious always describes an argument, claim, or piece of reasoning -- something that sounds convincing at first glance but falls apart once you check the evidence. It does not describe a person's manner of speaking (that's a different word, "glib").

Compare the words

Synonyms · words with a similar meaning

misleading: A misleading statement points its audience toward a wrong conclusion, and it can do so by accident — a mislabeled map misleads with no argument at all. Specious is narrower: it describes reasoning that looks right, a case built to survive a first glance and collapse under checking.

hollow: A hollow argument is one with nothing inside — you can usually hear the emptiness right away. A specious argument is more dangerous because the emptiness is disguised: it sounds right, cites its studies, and only collapses when someone checks. Hollow fails on contact; specious fools you first.

What it isn’t · antonyms and near-opposites

sound: (of an argument) well-founded and logically valid

valid: based on truth or correct reasoning

Where it sits · how actively it works to mislead — fallacious → specious → deceptive

fallacious vs. specious: Fallacious is less loaded than specious: a fallacious argument simply contains a mistake in reasoning, perhaps an honest one, while a specious argument wears a convincing surface that actively invites you to be fooled.

deceptive vs. specious: Deceptive is stronger than specious: a specious argument merely looks right on the surface, while deceptive packaging goes further, actively working to trick buyers about what they are getting.

Build the Word

The pieces

root — speci-

root — speci-: appearance, look (Latin (species))

suffix — -ous

suffix — -ous: full of, having the quality of (Latin (-osus))

Put it together

Put it together: Specious is built from the Latin root for 'appearance' plus the suffix -ous ('full of') -- so something specious is, quite literally, 'full of appearance': it looks right on the surface, even though it isn't.

Use the root in a new word: specimen

Use the root in a new word: specimen: The biology teacher passed around a preserved specimen of a monarch butterfly for the class to examine.

Root Check

Word Choice

Specious describes an argument, claim, or piece of reasoning that sounds plausible but doesn't hold up -- not a person's manner of speaking. Compare "glib," which describes how someone talks (smoothly, but insincerely). A person can deliver a specious argument in a perfectly serious, unhurried tone; specious is about whether the reasoning is sound, not about the speaker's style.
